title: Clothes from God (Genesis 3:14–24)
hookLine: even as they leave the garden, God makes them clothes

cards: Two people are standing in aprons made of fig leaves, sewn in a hurry on the afternoon everything went wrong. A fig leaf does the job for about a day. Then it dries, splits and crumbles.
Anyone who has patched a torn coat with tape knows the feeling: it holds, until it doesn't. That's what Adam and Eve are wearing when the consequences are spoken.
The end of the garden story is full of hard words: pain, sweat, thorns, dust. But tucked among them is one verse about sewing, and this time they're not the ones holding the needle.

teach.b: The consequences come first, and they're heavy. The serpent will crawl on its belly. The woman will have pain in childbirth.
The man will work cursed ground that brings up thorns. And then the line that many Christians hear on Ash Wednesday, in the King James Bible: "for dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return."
Only the serpent and the ground are cursed, not the man or the woman by name.
And in the middle of the hard words, there's a line many Christians call the first gospel: God tells the serpent that the woman's offspring will bruise its head.
Many Christians, from the early church on, have heard in it a promise of Jesus; Jewish readers have usually read it as the long struggle between people and evil. Then the man gives his wife a name.

teach.h: EVE: THE MOTHER OF ALL LIVING.
teach.b: Eve, in Hebrew Chavah, which sounds like the word for living, because she was the mother of all living. He names her life, right after hearing about death.
Then: "Unto Adam also and to his wife did the LORD God make coats of skins, and clothed them." They had made themselves flimsy aprons of fig leaves.
God makes them something that lasts. God, the potter of chapter two, now a tailor. Only then do they leave the garden, with cherubim and a flaming sword guarding the way to the tree of life.
The consequence stands. They don't go back. But they don't go out naked either.
Many readers say this is the story's pattern from here on: real consequences, and mercy that goes with them.

how: Christians read the end of Genesis 3 in different ways: many Western churches teach original sin from it, Orthodox Christians often speak of ancestral sin, and across traditions the clothing verse is preached as a picture of God's care after failure.

games.q: they've broken the one rule, and they must leave the garden. they're wearing aprons of fig leaves. what does God do before they go?
o: makes them coats of skins and clothes them.
lets them stay one more night.
games.why: the consequence stands; they don't go back. but God makes them something that lasts, and clothes them.

practice: Think of a time something went wrong because of your own choice, and the consequence was real: a job lost, a friendship strained, a scar.
Now look again, slowly, for a coat in the bag: someone who showed up anyway, a word at the right time, a door that opened later. If you pray, you can give thanks for it.
